newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan pulls no punches as HK handover looms.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan pulls no punches as HK handover looms.

text.p: As Hong Kong's return to Chinese sovereignty looms, Taipei is taking the opportunity to drive home the message that the Republic of China, founded in 1912, lives on in exile in Taiwan.
It has survived despite a diplomatic embargo that China's communists have steadily tightened since winning a civil war in 1949 and founding the People's Republic.
President Lee Teng-hui tried to make Taiwan's stand clear in a recent newspaper interview.

"While Beijing has persistently tried to shunt the Republic of China aside internationally, Republic of China citizens have become increasingly earnest about playing an active role in the world commensurate with Taiwan's political and economic success," Lee told the Washington Times.

Foreign Minister John Chang, who sidestepped China's embargo to address a European Parliament panel in May, flew to the United States on Sunday, kicking off Taiwan's latest drive to carve out a bit of its own space in the international arena.

"I will meet leaders of all spheres and enhance their understanding of the Republic of China, cross-strait relations and the whole situation. This should help the U.S. side in handling related issues," Chang said on his departure.
The "whole situation" that Chang spoke of will take a new focus in coming weeks as Beijing prepares to take Hong Kong back from Britain on July 1, ending 156 years of colonial rule.
Beijing has promised that Hong Kong will largely run itself under a "one country, two systems" model and has called this a dry run for China's reabsorption of a far bigger prize -- Taiwan.
Taipei, however, will have none of it.
The publicity surrounding Hong Kong's handover has enabled Taiwan and ruling Nationalist Party officials to express their opposition to "one country, two systems".
Lee, in a foretaste of the message his foreign minister will deliver in California and Colorado, said Hong Kong's retrocession, while welcome, was no guide for Taiwan.
"We believe that the United States fully realises the 'one country, two systems' scheme is not suitable for us and does not conform with the wishes of our people," Lee said.
Taiwan will mount live-fire war games on June 23-24, its biggest manoeuvres in three years and a rebuff to the United States.
Washington had called publicly for a postponement, saying holding war games at such a sensitive time -- a week before Hong Kong's handover -- would be "counterproductive".

Taiwan commanders, citing a need to give account to the electorate in the island's fledgling democracy, have said the manoeuvres would enable the military to show the public what kind of defensive systems their taxes have financed.
The island has repeatedly said the exercises are unrelated to Hong Kong's handover but a military spokesman last week confirmed the games were intended to boost public confidence.
Wary of being accused of being provocative, Taiwan's leaders have couched their actions in business-as-usual terms.
"My visit to the United States is absolutely unrelated to Hong Kong's handover," Chang said, describing its status as "absolutely unofficial and private".
"A lot of people have made excessive speculation...," he said.
Chang nonetheless acknowledged the political sensitivities.
"I hope everyone -- especially the mainland -- can view foreign visits made by related personnel of the Republic of China with an even mind," he said.
"I also hope they do not aggressively launch protests, because that would not have any benefit."
Only 30 countries, mostly undeveloped states in central America and Africa, recognise Taiwan rather than China.
The biggest of those, South Africa, is planning to switch allegiance to China later this year.
